items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewee mentions Elmo Hope only in the interviewer's question as an example of a player with a similar abstract style to Earl Hines; the interviewee does not mention any personal interaction or relationship with Elmo Hope.

ctx.x: anything on the thing?” Took it to the studio, and it was perfect. The sound, everything, was really great.

That’s interesting, because now, what we see . . . in a sense Earl also was a very abstract player, and I like, I use that term as opposed to free, because like you said you could see where it would develop out, seemingly out of nothing. Very embryonic stages and yet you started seeing little shapes of melodies and harmonies for the pieces. Having spoken to someone like Cecil Taylor, they feel like they’re following a tradition of Earl Hines, Duke Ellington, and Thelonious Monk, people like that, Elmo Hope, that…

I know when I first hear Earl, which was probably on a recording somewhere—I can’t really place it—he always seemed to me to be . . . Nobody said “far out” in those days. But it always had that quality of abstract . . . puzzle . . .
